plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: It gives facts I could check instead of guess. The 'This computer' section names the browsers, the WebGPU flags, Playwright's version and what is missing, and the hub link comes with a harness that returns a pass or fail. That let me build small engine spikes and write down verified settings, so builders don't have to rediscover them. I also liked the free choice of genre and perspective alongside firm rules on the things that matter: controller first at 10 feet, attract mode, dev sliders, no stubs.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Three things. First, 'for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own': it could mean the game only has to keep running outside a session (which is what the hub's check tests) or that it needs its own multiplayer. I planned for both by adding couch co-op. Second, TASK.md is written to a builder (package name, dev folder, chat reply, exit interview) while STAGE.md asks for a plan, so I had to infer which parts bind the planner; I treated them as the builder's. Third, the brief says to prefer file:// while the engine guide says ES modules don't load from file://. Inlining the module resolves this, but I only knew that after testing it.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Keeping the game original while still capturing the source. Much of what makes the source recognisable is its names, plot and specific operations, and the plan has to avoid all of those yet keep its feel, so I had to invent a new world, cast, disease and boss designs that still feel like the same genre and tone. A close second was scoping: the plan had to be large enough to show every mechanic but still buildable by agents I can't answer questions for, which is why it has a build order and an explicit cut order.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: Mark which sections apply to the planner and which to the builder. Define 'on its own' in one sentence. Say how long or detailed a plan should be, and whether engine spikes are welcome and where scratch files may go. Add -u to the example server command: `python3 -m http.server 0 --bind 127.0.0.1` doesn't flush its port line into a pipe, and a script reading it hangs, which cost me about fifteen minutes. It would also help to warn that the engine's bundled hero is a red-capped plumber, because 'use the native style' invites using it until you actually look at it.
